title: What Conditionals Do: Real vs Unreal
brief: Open by explaining the core communicative purpose of conditionals: they link a condition to a result. Establish the fundamental distinction between real conditions (situations the speaker treats as possible or likely) and unreal conditions (situations the speaker treats as hypothetical, contrary to fact, or impossible). Use your own example sentences to illustrate — for instance, a real condition such as 'If it rains, we cancel the match' versus an unreal one such as 'If I were a doctor, I would work in a clinic.' Explain that the real/unreal distinction, not the numbered label, is what learners need to grasp first. Do not yet introduce the full form tables; save those for the sections that follow.

title: Zero and First Conditionals: Conditions the Speaker Believes Are Real
brief: Cover the zero conditional (if + present simple, present simple) and the first conditional (if + present simple, will + infinitive) as the two patterns used for real or genuinely possible conditions. For the zero conditional, explain its use for general truths and automatic results, e.g. 'If you heat water to 100°C, it boils' and 'If customers complain, the manager calls them back.' For the first conditional, explain its use for specific future possibilities the speaker considers likely or at least plausible, e.g. 'If she studies tonight, she will pass the test.' Note that 'when' can replace 'if' in zero conditionals without changing meaning, but not always in first conditionals. Include a brief note on common spoken contractions such as 'she'll' and 'we'll.' Keep the focus on form and meaning together; do not yet address teaching strategies.

title: Second and Third Conditionals: Unreal and Counterfactual Conditions
brief: Explain the second conditional (if + past simple, would + infinitive) for present or future unreal situations — things the speaker imagines but does not expect, e.g. 'If I lived near the coast, I would swim every morning' — and for advice-giving, e.g. 'If I were you, I would apologise.' Address the 'were' vs 'was' question directly: 'were' is the traditional and still widely taught form for all persons in formal and written English, while 'was' is common in informal speech; teachers should know both. Then cover the third conditional (if + past perfect, would have + past participle) for past unreal situations — things that did not happen, e.g. 'If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train.' Emphasise that the third conditional is inherently retrospective and often carries emotional weight such as regret or relief. Use your own contrasting sentence pairs to show how second and third conditionals differ in time reference.

title: Mixed Conditionals: Crossing Time Frames
brief: Introduce mixed conditionals as combinations that cross time frames, most commonly a past condition with a present result (if + past perfect, would + infinitive), e.g. 'If she had taken that job in Berlin, she would be fluent in German by now,' and a present condition with a past result (if + past simple, would have + past participle), e.g. 'If he were more careful, he would not have made that mistake.' Explain clearly why each example crosses time frames and what meaning that creates. Acknowledge that mixed conditionals are less frequent in everyday speech and are typically introduced at upper-intermediate or advanced level. Caution writers against presenting mixed conditionals as a single fixed pattern, since the combinations depend on the speaker's intended meaning. Do not introduce teaching activities here; keep this section focused on form and meaning.

title: Beyond the Canonical Forms: Variations Teachers Should Know
brief: Address the grammatical variations that exist within each conditional type and that teachers will encounter in authentic language. Cover: (1) modals other than 'will' and 'would' in the result clause, such as 'might,' 'could,' and 'should,' e.g. 'If you ask her, she might help' or 'If I had more time, I could finish this'; (2) continuous and perfect aspects in the condition clause, e.g. 'If she has already left, we will need to call her'; (3) the use of 'unless,' 'provided that,' 'as long as,' and 'on condition that' as alternatives to 'if,' with brief notes on how their meaning differs slightly; and (4) inverted conditionals in formal writing, e.g. 'Were I to resign, the project would collapse' and 'Had they arrived on time, the meeting would have started.' The goal is to equip teachers to handle real-world language without being thrown by deviation from the four-type template.

title: Teaching Conditionals: Keeping the Rules from Becoming a Maze
brief: Offer practical classroom guidance grounded in the grammar covered in previous sections. Begin by recommending that teachers introduce conditionals through meaning and context before presenting the form table — for example, starting with a relatable scenario such as a job interview or a travel plan and eliciting the conditional naturally. Suggest sequencing: zero and first before second and third, with mixed conditionals reserved for higher levels. Recommend using timeline diagrams or a simple two-column 'condition / result' chart to help learners see the structure without memorising labels. Address the common learner error of using 'would' in the if-clause ('If I would go…') and explain why it is non-standard in most conditional types, while noting the rare exception in polite requests ('If you would take a seat…'). Suggest that drilling isolated sentences is less effective than having learners produce conditionals in response to genuine communicative prompts, such as giving advice, speculating about news stories, or discussing past decisions. Close by reminding teachers that the numbered system is a teaching scaffold, not a description of how speakers think.
